title: Reducing Decoding Latency in Quantum Error Correction by Early Starting Clustering
authors: Tommaso Peduzzi, Lukas Bödeker, Markus Müller, Luis Colmenarez
abstract: In quantum error correction, fast low-latency decoding is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as delays in processing syndrome data can lead to the backlog problem. Existing decoders, including parallelizable approaches such as Union-Find, begin decoding only after all stabilizer measurement outcomes from an error-correction cycle have been received, inherently introducing a delay before decoding begins. We introduce Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG), a modification of the Union-Find decoder that processes syndrome information during stabilizer measurements by clustering and correcting errors as they appear. This approach reduces the size of the remaining decoding problem at the end of the quantum error correction cycle and, consequently, the time required to complete the decoding process. While this early start of clustering incurs a modest reduction in decoding accuracy, it preserves the decoder's scalability. Surface-code simulations show that the resulting reduction in post-measurement idling can outweigh the accuracy loss, yielding an improved speed-accuracy trade-off. These results demonstrate that real-time, early-starting decoding during QEC cycles is both feasible and can be advantageous for quantum error correction. Demonstrated here for the surface code, CAYG is broadly applicable to other quantum error-correcting codes, which allow for clustering-based decoding approaches, and is extensible to dedicated real-time decoding hardware.
summary: This paper introduces Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG), a novel decoding algorithm for Quantum Error Correction that processes syndrome data incrementally as measurements occur. By enabling early, real-time decoding, CAYG significantly reduces latency compared to methods that wait for all measurements. This demonstrates a feasible path toward faster, more practical fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The primary challenge is reducing the decoding latency in Quantum Error Correction (QEC) to enable fault-tolerant quantum computation and avoid the syndrome data backlog problem.
main_result: The proposed Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) decoder enables real-time, early-starting decoding by processing syndrome information concurrently with measurements, achieving an improved speed-accuracy trade-off.
method: CAYG modifies the Union-Find decoder by allowing cluster formation and error correction to begin incrementally as syndrome measurements arrive, rather than waiting for the entire set of measurements to complete.
model_or_system: The work is primarily demonstrated on the surface code, a topological stabilizer code implemented on a 2D lattice. Decoding involves finding a minimum-weight perfect matching on a graph representing syndrome defects.
key_observables: Decoding latency, decoding accuracy, logical error probability (p_L), and the effective distance of the code.
important_parameters: The cluster lifetime parameter ($l$), which controls the temporal buffer for merging defects, and the error rates ($p_{	ext{data}}, p_{	ext{meas}}$).
main_assumptions: The standard Union-Find decoder assumes access to the complete syndrome history; CAYG introduces a trade-off by committing corrections based on partial information.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between standard sequential decoding (UF) and pipelined CAYG decoding, showing how CAYG processes data streams in real-time, and detail the failure mechanisms in staircase chains when the temporal buffer ($l$) is set to zero.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the latency bottleneck in QEC decoding. It then introduces CAYG as a temporal parallelization technique extending the Union-Find decoder. Subsequent analysis focuses on the role of the cluster lifetime parameter ($l$) to balance speed against the risk of premature, inaccurate error correction.
why_interesting: While focused on QEC, the concept of pipelining computation with data acquisition—processing results immediately rather than batching them—is highly relevant to designing real-time control systems for quantum hardware.
